query: Consider a single-crystal FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy subjected to uniaxial tensile loading in the elastic-to-plastic transition regime. The material exhibits a yield strength that appears anomalously insensitive to strain rates compared to traditional metals, despite high strain rates leading to significant dislocation accumulation. The operating regime includes temperatures ranging from cryogenic to elevated (up to 600 K). What is the dominant mechanism driving the onset of yielding (e.g., dislocation nucleation at specific defects vs. thermal activation)? Identify the design constraints regarding crystal orientation anisotropy and propose a boundary condition test to falsify the hypothesis that FCC-to-BCC phase transformation is the primary deformation mode.

generation.hypothesis: In single-crystal FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) within the elastic-to-plastic transition regime, the onset of yielding is primarily driven by thermally activated dislocation nucleation at surface defects and stacking fault nucleation, rather than FCC-to-BCC phase transformation. The anomalously low strain-rate sensitivity of yield strength arises from the high activation energy barriers for dislocation motion in the highly distorted lattice, which are overcome by thermal fluctuations rather than stress-assisted mechanisms. The dominant deformation mode involves twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and martensitic transformation to HCP (not BCC) phases, facilitated by low stacking fault energy. Crystal orientation anisotropy dictates the critical resolved shear stress for partial dislocation nucleation, with <111> orientations exhibiting higher yield strength due to multiple slip system activation barriers. The FCC-to-BCC transformation hypothesis is falsified because the alloy maintains FCC stability up to 600 K under uniaxial tension, with HCP martensite forming only under high strain or cryogenic conditions via stacking fault accumulation.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy with FCC crystal structure, low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ/m²), and no pre-existing BCC phase.
generation.intervention: Uniaxial tensile loading in the elastic-to-plastic transition regime at strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10² s⁻¹, with temperatures from 77 K to 600 K.
generation.conditions: Cryogenic to elevated temperatures (77–600 K), single-crystal orientation control, uniaxial tensile stress state, strain rates covering elastic-to-plastic transition.
generation.structural_mediator: Stacking faults and deformation twins acting as precursors to HCP martensitic transformation; dislocation nucleation sites at free surfaces and grain boundaries (in polycrystalline analogs).
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated nucleation of partial dislocations leading to stacking fault formation, followed by twinning and HCP martensitic transformation. The low strain-rate sensitivity is due to the dominance of thermal activation over stress-driven dislocation glide in the high-drag lattice.
generation.predicted_outcome: Yield strength will show minimal dependence on strain rate (low strain-rate sensitivity exponent) but strong temperature dependence. HCP phase fraction will increase with decreasing temperature and increasing strain, while BCC phase will remain absent. Crystal orientation will significantly affect yield strength, with <111> orientations showing higher yield points.
generation.baseline: Traditional FCC metals (e.g., Cu, Al) exhibit higher strain-rate sensitivity due to easier dislocation glide and lower activation barriers.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis holds for single-crystal FCC FeNiCrMn HEAs up to 600 K; fails if BCC phase forms under tension or if strain-rate sensitivity exceeds typical HEA values (>0.02).
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the exact activation energy values for dislocation nucleation and the role of magnetic ordering at cryogenic temperatures. The transition temperature between thermally activated and athermal regimes may vary with crystal orientation.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform in-situ high-resolution XRD during uniaxial tensile testing of single-crystal FeNiCrMn HEA at 300 K and 600 K while varying strain rates (10⁻⁴ to 10² s⁻¹). Monitor for the emergence of BCC phase peaks. If BCC peaks appear and correlate with yield strength changes, the hypothesis is falsified. Additionally, measure yield strength vs. strain rate; if sensitivity exceeds 0.02, the thermal activation mechanism is insufficient.

Conversely, high-pressure studies remain a virgin area in HEAs. In this work, using in situ high-pressure XRD techniques, we observed the first polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as shown in Fig. 1c . Therefore, some critical questions are how and why can an hcp HEA form at high-pressure and can it be maintained at ambient conditions? According to the d -spacing of the main reflections of both fcc and hcp (that is, (111) and (220) of fcc , and (100), (002), (101) and (110) of hcp , as a function of pressure shown in Fig. 2a ), it is clear that the hcp -(002) and hcp -(110) planes inherit the fcc -(111) and fcc -(220) planes, respectively. In addition, Fig. 2b shows no obvious volume collapse during the transition; both the fcc and hcp phases seem to have almost the same volume per atom and bulk modulus. 3.1. Deformation Behavior of Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs

Figure 2 shows the stress–strain curves of the Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs at 77, 300, and 1000 K respectively. At 77 K, Ag NW deforms via nucleation and propagation of a partial dislocation from the free surface, leaving a stacking fault inside the NW (see Figure 3 a). As deformation continues, the stacking fault further separates into two twin boundaries, which extend and continue to grow through entire NW. The cross-section area of the NW eventually converts from (110) to (100), resulting in two peaks in the SS curve, as shown in Figure 2 a. The area between two twin boundaries is transformed as also shown in Figure 3 a between 8% to 32% elongation in the Ag NW. The phase transformation is mainly driven by the surface stresses which enable the reduction in surface energy in the nanowire. On further loading, the difference between two boundaries decreases and finally vanishes at around 50% elongation, resulting in an improved work hardening.
